subsystems.name: Dynamic ring core
subsystems.role: a continuous cable loop circling the Earth above orbital speed — its excess centrifugal force is what holds everything up.

subsystems.name: Stationary sheath
subsystems.role: the non-rotating outer structure that rides on the ring and carries tracks, power and payloads.

subsystems.name: Maglev coupling and linear motors
subsystems.role: support the sheath against the ring and keep the ring spinning by replacing energy lost to friction and drag.

subsystems.name: Ground and space tethers
subsystems.role: hang from the ring to the surface, or upward to higher orbits, so payloads can climb rather than be launched.

subsystems.name: Energy system
subsystems.role: supplies the megawatts needed to overcome losses in a 40,000 km loop.
parts: ground power connection or beamed power

subsystems.name: Assembly, control and station keeping
subsystems.role: build the ring in space and keep it stable against perturbations.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate the physics small
buildSteps.detail: Fly a ring a few tens of metres across in low Earth orbit: a spinning loop magnetically levitated inside a static sheath. The aim is measured stability, gap control and how fast the loop loses speed.

buildSteps.title: Solve the material question
buildSteps.detail: The moving ring is in near-free orbit, so it does not need exotic cable — but any tether hanging from 300 km must carry its own weight, needing a specific strength around 3 million N·m per kg, which only the best carbon fibre approaches. That sets the whole design.

buildSteps.title: Get mass to orbit cheaply
buildSteps.detail: Tens of thousands of tonnes of cable, magnets and structure are needed; either launch costs fall by a large factor or most material is mined and processed off-world.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the ring in orbit
buildSteps.detail: Robots join cable segments into a closed loop at roughly 250–300 km altitude, above most atmospheric drag but still within reach of ground tethers. Joining must preserve balance, since an uneven ring wobbles.

buildSteps.title: Spin it up
buildSteps.detail: Linear motors accelerate the loop until it moves faster than local orbital velocity, so its outward push exceeds gravity. Only then can a stationary structure be hung on it.

buildSteps.title: Attach the stationary sheath
buildSteps.detail: Magnetic units clamp the sheath to the passing ring. The ring pulls inward on the sheath and the sheath holds the ring down — a balance that must be actively controlled every second.

buildSteps.title: Run ground tethers
buildSteps.detail: Cables are lowered from the ring to anchor points on the surface. From this moment payloads can be lifted from the ground to the ring by climbers instead of rockets.

buildSteps.title: Add climbers and power
buildSteps.detail: Electric climbers carry cargo up the tethers, and power feeds replace the energy the ring bleeds away, turning the structure into working infrastructure.

buildSteps.title: Extend into a network
buildSteps.detail: Additional rings at different inclinations, and tethers reaching to higher orbits, give access to any latitude and remove the need to launch from the ground at all.

prerequisites.why: carbon fibre is close to the limit for a 300 km tether; reaching higher orbits needs carbon-nanotube-class fibres that exist only as laboratory samples.

prerequisites.tech: Very low-cost launch or off-world material
prerequisites.why: the ring's mass is far beyond any single structure built so far, so it must be launched cheaply or built from lunar or asteroid material.

prerequisites.tech: Maglev at orbital relative speed in vacuum
prerequisites.why: no machine has ever levitated a guideway at several kilometres per second; today's maglev trains run at roughly a hundredth of that.
the ring can only be closed by many coordinated robots working without humans present.
a ring this large is unstable in several modes and must be steered continuously for decades.
most of the ring's energy circulates internally, but losses must be replaced continuously.

pathway.milestone: conceptual studies and small tethered and maglev experiments
pathway.unlocks: confidence that a levitated loop can be held stable at all.

pathway.milestone: a metre-to-kilometre test ring in low Earth orbit
pathway.unlocks: measured losses, control laws and material data — the first real engineering numbers.

pathway.milestone: a single uncrewed ring at 250–300 km with ground tethers
pathway.unlocks: payload delivery to orbit by climbing rather than launching, at a fraction of rocket cost.

pathway.milestone: a network of rings at several inclinations plus tethers to higher orbits
pathway.unlocks: routine, high-volume movement of people and cargo off Earth — far beyond what chemical rockets can sustain.
